newsitem.title: LATVIA: INTERVIEW - AIR BALTIC PLANS TO BREAK EVEN IN 1997.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - AIR BALTIC PLANS TO BREAK EVEN IN 1997.

text.p: Latvian airline Air Baltic, which is nearly a third owned by Scandinavian Airlines, on Monday said it would break even on operating flights in 1997.

"In 1997 we plan to break even in operating flights, while the investment programme continues in 1997 and in the first half of 1998," Oleg Korshe, Air Baltic's Senior Vice President, told Reuters in an interview.
The company has not revealed any profit or loss figures since coming into existence in late 1995, but it said it made a loss in its first year of business.
He added that the company's passenger turnover is expected to grow to 170,000 in 1997 from 115,000 in 1996.
Air Baltic is not optimistic about the total passenger turnover growth in Riga airport during 1997, but sees its own turnover growing faster.
"We are taking over passengers from other carriers by offering them more convenient flight times and better co-ordination with flights from other centres," Korshe said.
"The aim of 1996 was to create a western-style air carrier, and this aim was completed," he said.
"We are not planning much in terms of new flights this year, but we keep in mind Moscow and St. Petersburg," he added.
Air Baltic is currently not granted flying rights to Russia, which links the now insolvent former Latvian carrier debt issue with flying rights.
"According to our calculations we are short 40,000 passengers per year, who would fly to Russia.
"There is only one way for a small air carrier and that is to look for natural passenger flows on a regional level," Korshe said.
"We are going to optimize existing routes in order to get the most out of them," he added.
Air Baltic says it is ready to enter the EU market both in terms of technical and operational standards.
"We are already flying a Geneva-Copenhagen route and as soon as the necessary political decisions are in place, we will be ready to take part in the EU market," Korshe said.
Air Baltic's 1996 results are expected to be announced following a managers' meeting on March 20.
SAS has a 29 percent stake in the company and Swedfund and the Danish Investment Fund also own stakes.
